opus-5.5.text:
What strikes me most is how much they can do without language. When you watch chimpanzees, they use tools, they plan, they cooperate, they deceive each other, they even have something like politics within the group. There's that famous working-memory experiment from Kyoto where young chimps see numbers flash on a screen for a fraction of a second, and they can recall the positions far better than most humans can. So in some narrow perceptual and memory tasks, they actually beat us.

For me, as someone working on vision and AI, that's a really important reminder. A lot of people today assume intelligence basically equals language, because large language models have been so successful. But chimps show you that a huge amount of intelligence lives in perception, in understanding the physical world, in acting in an environment, in modeling other agents. None of that needs words. Language sits on top, maybe as a compression or communication layer, but the foundation is this grounded, visual, embodied understanding.

So when I think about where AI should go, chimpanzees make me ask: we've built systems that can talk very fluently, but do we have anything that understands the world the way a chimp does, that can look at a scene, figure out how things work, and use that to act? I don't think we're there yet. That gap is, to me, one of the most interesting problems right now.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most is how much chimpanzees can do without language. When I look at a chimp solving a problem, say using a stick to fish for termites, or remembering where fruit trees are across a huge forest and when they'll ripen, that's genuine planning and spatial reasoning. There's no symbolic system underneath it. It's all grounded in perception, in the body, in direct interaction with the physical world.

That's very relevant to how I think about AI right now. Most of the progress we've seen in the last few years has come through language. Large language models are extremely impressive, but they learned about the world through text, which is a very compressed, very human-filtered description of reality. A chimpanzee never read anything, and yet it has a far richer model of physical space, of objects, of cause and effect, than any of our current systems. If you drop a chimp into a new environment it adapts. Our models tend to break.

So for me, chimps are a kind of existence proof. They show that a lot of what we'd call intelligence, the core of it, can be built from vision and action alone. Language in humans sits on top of that foundation. It doesn't replace it. And I think the field has, in some sense, gotten the order backwards. We built the top floor first, the language part, and now we're trying to go back and build the foundation, the visual and physical understanding.

The other thing that strikes me is efficiency. A chimp learns all of this from a few years of experience, with a brain that runs on roughly the power of a light bulb. We're training models on more data than any animal could experience in thousands of lifetimes, and they still don't have that kind of robust common sense about the world. So when I look at chimpanzee intelligence, I don't see something primitive. I see a very hard, very unsolved problem that we haven't cracked yet.

astra-6.text:
What strikes me is how much intelligence they demonstrate without language like ours. They can use tools, learn from one another, and navigate complicated social relationships. It makes you question whether language is the right lens for understanding all of intelligence.

From an AI perspective, I find that fascinating. A chimpanzee learns by seeing, moving, and interacting with the world. That raises a question for me: how much of intelligence comes from that direct experience, and what might we miss if we focus too narrowly on language?
